definition: AlphaGeometry is an artificial intelligence (AI) program that can solve hard problems in Euclidean geometry.
details: The system comprises a data-driven large language model (LLM) and a rule-based symbolic engine (Deductive Database Arithmetic Reasoning). It was developed by DeepMind, a subsidiary of Google. The program solved 25 geometry problems out of 30 from the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) under competition time limits—a performance almost as good as the average human gold medallist. For comparison, the previous AI program, called Wu's method, managed to solve only 10 problems. DeepMind published a paper about AlphaGeometry in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on 17 January 2024. AlphaGeometry was featured in MIT Technology Review on the same day. Traditional geometry programs are symbolic engines that rely exclusively on human-coded rules to generate rigorous proofs, which makes them lack flexibility in unusual situations. AlphaGeometry combines such a symbolic engine with a specialized large language model trained on synthetic data of geometrical proofs. When the symbolic engine doesn't manage to find a formal and rigorous proof on its own, it solicits the large language model, which suggests a geometrical construct to move forward. explainer.lead: AlphaGeometry is DeepMind's AI system for proving difficult Euclidean geometry problems. It pairs creative suggestions from a language model with a symbolic engine that keeps proofs rigorous, solving 25 out of 30 International Mathematical Olympiad problems under competition time limits.

tiers.eli5: Imagine solving a shape puzzle with a strict rule book and a clever helper. The rule book checks every step, while the helper suggests drawing an extra line or point when you get stuck. AlphaGeometry works this way, combining imaginative hints with careful checking to produce geometry proofs.
tiers.practitioner: Use it as a neuro-symbolic theorem prover rather than a general-purpose chatbot: the language model proposes auxiliary constructions, while Deductive Database Arithmetic Reasoning performs formal deduction. AlphaGeometry 2 uses a fine-tuned Gemini model for constructions and autoformalization, and expands the representation language to cover 88% of IMO geometry questions from 2000 to 2024. Do not assume direct transfer to other mathematics, because the approach depends on domain-specific rules and synthetic data.
tiers.paperLevel: AlphaGeometry is a neuro-symbolic theorem prover for Euclidean geometry: a language model trained on synthetic geometric proofs proposes auxiliary constructions, while Deductive Database Arithmetic Reasoning (DDAR) performs rule-based deduction. DeepMind's Nature paper appeared on 17 January 2024, and the system solved 25 of 30 IMO problems under competition time limits. Its broader applicability remains uncertain because symbolic engines require domain-specific rules and the language model requires synthetic training data.

explainer.example: For a geometry problem whose proof requires an extra point, DDAR first tries to derive the result from the given diagram. If it stalls, the language model can suggest adding that point or an auxiliary line; DDAR then checks the resulting deductions and continues the formal proof search.

explainer.intuition: Hard geometry proofs often hinge on spotting an extra line or point that makes the solution possible. Human-coded rules are rigorous but can be rigid, while a language model can suggest useful constructions without supplying the formal proof itself. AlphaGeometry divides the work between these two strengths.
howItWorks: Train a specialized language model on synthetic geometric proofs.
Let the DDAR symbolic engine attempt a formal proof using its rules.
When deduction stalls, ask the language model for an auxiliary construction.
Add the suggested point or line and resume symbolic deduction.
Continue until the symbolic engine establishes a rigorous proof.
explainer.whyItMatters: AlphaGeometry shows that learned suggestions and rule-based proof checking can work together on problems where neither creativity nor rigor is enough alone. Its 25-out-of-30 result approached the performance of an average human IMO gold medallist on that test.
misconceptions: It is not just a language model: DDAR supplies the rule-based formal deduction.
Solving 25 of 30 IMO geometry problems does not mean it can solve all of mathematics.
AlphaGeometry 2 is an expanded system published on 5 February 2025, not the original 2024 result.
